mainTopic: The היקש between נזירות and נדרים (בל תאחר and הפרה), and שמואל on 'מודר אני ממך'
overview: The amud opens by finishing a discussion of a ברייתא that links נזירות to נדרים by a היקש. The ברייתא uses that link to apply בל תאחר to a נזיר's קרבנות. The גמרא gives two reasons the link is needed: a נזיר is finished after shaving with just one קרבן, and his קרבנות cannot be taken on through a נדר. It defends the second reason by comparing the נזיר's חטאת to the חטאת חלב and the חטאת of a יולדת. Next it asks why a היקש is needed to teach that a father or husband can cancel נזירות. The answer is that נזירות has a fixed length, so we could not have learned this from נדרים alone. The גמרא then returns to the משנה's phrase 'מודר אני ממך' and quotes שמואל, who seems to say it works only with the added words 'that which I eat of yours.' Two ברייתות challenge that reading. In the end the גמרא rereads שמואל: the eating words explain why only the speaker is forbidden while his friend stays permitted.

steps.title: Shaving after one offering might have suggested no delay violation
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its first answer: because a נזיר is done once he shaves after just one of his three קרבנות, we might have thought he does not violate בל תאחר for the others, so the היקש teaches that he does.
steps.simpleTranslation: And since if he shaved after bringing one of the three offerings he has fulfilled his duty, one might think he does not violate 'Do not delay' for the rest. So the verse teaches us that he does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is completing its answer to why the ברייתא needs a היקש to apply בל תאחר to a נזיר's קרבנות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נזיר brings three קרבנות: an עולה, a חטאת and a שלמים. Since shaving after even one of them ends his נזירות, the other two might seem unimportant, as if delaying them breaks no rule. The היקש tells us that בל תאחר still applies to them.

keyTerms.meaning: He shaved (the נזיר's shaving at the end of his term)
Of the three of them (the three קרבנות of a נזיר)
He has fulfilled his duty
The prohibition against delaying the bringing of a vowed or owed offering
It teaches us (something we would not have known)

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם גִּילַּח עַל אַחַת מִשְּׁלׇשְׁתָּן — יָצָא,
phrases.english: and since if he shaved on one of the three, he has fulfilled his duty,
phrases.notes: The three are the נזיר's עולה, חטאת and שלמים.

phrases.english: one might think he should not violate 'You shall not delay' on account of it,
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes an answer that began before this section
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies a reason one might have thought בל תאחר does not apply
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since shaving after one קרבן ends the נזירות, delaying the others is no violation
steps.terutzMaskana: בל תאחר applies to all of a נזיר's קרבנות

steps.title: Second answer: a נזיר's offerings cannot be taken on by a vow
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers another reason the היקש is needed: a נזיר's קרבנות are not something a person can take on through a נדר, so we might have thought בל תאחר does not apply to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you prefer, say: what is new about it? That a person cannot take on these offerings through a vow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different explanation of why the היקש is needed for בל תאחר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בל תאחר is usually connected to things a person promised to bring. A נזיר's קרבנות cannot be taken on through a נדר; they come automatically with being a נזיר. So without the היקש we might have said the rule against delay does not cover them.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces another answer)
Its novelty; what is unusual about it
Taking it on through a vow

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
What is its novelty?
Because one cannot take it on through a vow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the same question
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a unique feature of a נזיר's קרבנות
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Offerings that cannot be vowed are not covered by בל תאחר
steps.terutzMaskana: The היקש is needed to apply בל תאחר to them

steps.title: Why the fat sin-offering is different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא heads off an expected challenge. A חטאת חלב also cannot be vowed, yet בל תאחר applies to it. The answer is that it brings כפרה, while a נזיר's חטאת brings no כפרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And as for what bothers you about the sin-offering for eating forbidden fat: that offering comes to bring atonement. But what does the נזיר's sin-offering come for?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends its second answer against a likely question before anyone asks it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חטאת חלב cannot be vowed either, and still you may not delay it. That might seem to defeat the second answer. The difference is that a חטאת חלב brings כפרה, so of course it must not be delayed, while a נזיר's חטאת does not atone for any sin.

keyTerms.meaning: A sin-offering brought for accidentally eating forbidden fat
Atonement
What does it come for?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא דְּקָא קַשְׁיָא לָךְ חַטַּאת חֵלֶב —
phrases.english: And as for what is difficult for you, the sin-offering for forbidden fat:
phrases.notes: The worry is that a חטאת חלב also can't be vowed, yet delaying it is forbidden.

phrases.english: the sin-offering for fat comes for atonement.
The sin-offering of a nazirite, what does it come for?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends step 2 against a challenge it expects
steps.terutzHavaAmina: חטאת חלב shows that offerings which cannot be vowed are still covered by בל תאחר
steps.terutzMaskana: חטאת חלב is different because it brings כפרה

steps.title: Challenge from the sin-offering of a woman after childbirth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the distinction from step 3: a יולדת's חטאת also brings no כפרה, yet בל תאחר applies to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But look at the sin-offering of a woman who gave birth. It does not come for atonement, and yet she violates 'Do not delay' if she holds it back!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the 'atonement' distinction with a case that does not fit it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If בל תאחר applied only to atoning offerings, it would not apply to a יולדת's חטאת. But it does apply. So lack of כפרה cannot be what makes a נזיר's חטאת seem exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: But look at (introduces a counter-example)
The sin-offering of a woman who gave birth

phrases.aramaic: וַהֲרֵי חַטַּאת יוֹלֶדֶת דְּלָא אָתְיָא לְכַפָּרָה,
phrases.english: But there is the sin-offering of a woman after childbirth, which does not come for atonement,
and one violates 'You shall not delay' with it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the distinction made in step 3
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a חטאת which brings no כפרה might be free of בל תאחר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Counter-example: a יולדת's חטאת brings no כפרה, yet בל תאחר applies

steps.title: The childbirth offering permits eating sacred food
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: a יולדת's חטאת at least allows her to eat קדשים, while a נזיר's חטאת accomplishes neither כפרה nor permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: That offering allows her to eat sacred food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing that the יולדת's offering does something important.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even without bringing כפרה, the יולדת's חטאת makes something allowed: she may eat קדשים again. A נזיר's חטאת neither atones nor permits anything. That is why it was a real חידוש, and why the היקש is needed for it.

keyTerms.meaning: Permits
Sacred, consecrated food

steps.whatToRemember: The second answer stands: a נזיר's חטאת cannot be vowed, does not atone and does not permit anything. Without the היקש we might have thought בל תאחר does not apply to it.

phrases.english: That one permits her
to eat consecrated food.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: A יולדת's חטאת is just like a נזיר's because neither atones
steps.terutzMaskana: A יולדת's חטאת permits קדשים; a נזיר's does nothing of the kind, so it needs the היקש

steps.title: The ברייתא: father and husband cancel נזירות like ordinary נדרים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next part of the ברייתא: just as a father or husband can cancel נדרים, they can also cancel נזירות.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: Just as with vows a father cancels his daughter's vows and a husband cancels his wife's vows, so too with nazirite vows, a father cancels his daughter's and a husband cancels his wife's.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting the next line of the ברייתא to set up a question about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This part of the ברייתא uses the same היקש to teach that הפרה, the power of a father or husband to cancel, works for נזירות just as it does for נדרים. The גמרא quotes it here so it can look closely at it.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said (quoting an earlier source)
Cancels a vow (הפרה)
The vow to become a נזיר

phrases.english: The Master said:
Just as with vows,
a father cancels his daughter's vows
and a husband cancels his wife's vows,
so too with naziriteship,
a father cancels his daughter's naziriteship
and a husband cancels his wife's naziriteship.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next clause of the same ברייתא
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Through the היקש, a father or husband can cancel נזירות just as they cancel נדרים

steps.title: Why a juxtaposition when a simple comparison would work?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a היקש is needed for this. We could learn it from נדרים through a מה מצינו comparison.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need the juxtaposition? Let it come through 'what do we find' from vows!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the need for the היקש in the case of הפרה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A היקש is a strong link made directly by the פסוק. If we can already learn that נזירות can be cancelled by comparing it to ordinary נדרים, the היקש seems unnecessary. The גמרא will need to explain what extra thing the היקש teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need?
היקש: a link made by placing two topics together in a פסוק
"What do we find": learning one case from a similar one

phrases.english: Why do I need the juxtaposition?
Let it come through 'what do we find' from vows!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the source given in step 6
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for a היקש to teach הפרה of נזירות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A simpler comparison, מה מצינו from נדרים, would be enough

steps.title: Why the היקש is needed: נזירות has a time limit
steps.stepSummary: Without the היקש, we might think הפרה works only for נדרים, which have no time limit. נזירות has a set length (thirty days by default), so we might think it cannot be cancelled.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps he can cancel only נדרים, because they have no time limit. But נזירות has a limit, since plain נזירות lasts thirty days, so I would say he cannot cancel it. The היקש teaches us that he can.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 7. It explains why a simple מה מצינו from נדרים would not be enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נדר can last forever, so it makes sense that a father or husband could step in and cancel it. נזירות ends by itself after a fixed time (plain נזירות is thirty days), so we might think there is less reason to allow cancelling it. The היקש tells us that הפרה works for נזירות too.

keyTerms.meaning: A fixed limit or end point
Plain נזירות taken without stating a length, which lasts thirty days
It teaches us (the source tells us something we would not have known)
He cancels (does הפרה)

steps.whatToRemember: The היקש between נדרים and נזירות is needed because נזירות has a fixed length. Without the היקש, that difference could have stopped us from learning הפרה of נזירות from נדרים.

phrases.english: Perhaps it is only with vows that he can cancel
phrases.notes: 'He' is the father or husband from step 6.

phrases.english: because a vow has no fixed limit

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל גַּבֵּי נְזִירוּת דְּאִית לֵיהּ קִיצּוּתָא
phrases.english: but with נזירות, which has a fixed limit
since plain נזירות is thirty days
I would say no, he cannot cancel it
so the היקש teaches us that he can

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 7 by showing a weakness in the מה מצינו.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points out a difference (פירכא) that would block the מה מצינו, so the היקש is necessary.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since נזירות has a time limit, we might think a father or husband cannot cancel it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The היקש shows that הפרה works for נזירות just as it works for נדרים.

steps.title: שמואל: 'I am avowed from you' needs the words about eating
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of 'מודר אני'. שמואל says none of these phrases work until the person adds 'that which I eat of yours' or 'that which I taste of yours'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: one who says to his friend 'I am avowed from you,' and so on. שמואל said: in all these cases, it works only once he says 'that which I eat of yours' or 'that which I taste of yours.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It quotes a line from the משנה and brings שמואל's rule about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying only 'I am avowed from you' does not make clear what is forbidden. According to שמואל, it does not even count as a hint of a נדר until the person names the eating or tasting. Once he does, the נדר takes effect.

keyTerms.meaning: I am avowed (forbidden by a vow)
An early אמורא of בבל
That which I eat of yours
That which I taste of yours

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule shapes the rest of the section. Each ברייתא that follows is tested against it.

phrases.english: "One who says to his friend: I am avowed from you, etc."
שמואל said:
In all of them, it does not work until he says
"that which I eat of yours"
or "that which I taste of yours"

steps.triggerLanguage: הָאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵירוֹ מוּדָּר אֲנִי וְכוּ׳ אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, going back to the wording in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'מודר אני ממך' and similar phrases work only if the person adds 'שאני אוכל לך' or 'שאני טועם לך'.

steps.title: A ברייתא lists 'I am avowed from you' as working by itself
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists 'I am avowed from you' and similar phrases as forbidding him. It lists the eating and tasting phrases separately. This suggests each list works alone, which goes against שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: 'I am avowed from you,' 'I am separated from you,' 'I am distanced from you': he is forbidden. 'That which I eat of yours,' 'that which I taste of yours': he is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל from a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says 'he is forbidden' after the first group of phrases, before the eating phrases are even mentioned. That makes it look as if 'I am avowed from you' works by itself, which goes against שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: They challenged (from a תנאי source such as a ברייתא)
I am separated
I am distanced
He is forbidden

phrases.english: They challenged from a ברייתא:
"I am avowed from you"
"I am separated from you," "I am distanced from you"
he is forbidden
"that which I eat of yours," "that which I taste of yours"
he is forbidden!

steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's rule that 'מודר אני ממך' needs the eating phrase added.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says 'forbidden' right after the first list, so those phrases seem to work by themselves.

steps.title: Reading the ברייתא's second part as explaining the first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the second half of the ברייתא as explaining the first. 'I am avowed from you' works only when he says 'that which I eat of yours' or 'that which I taste of yours'.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what the ברייתא means: when are these words said? When he says 'that which I eat of yours' or 'that which I taste of yours.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It explains that the second line of the ברייתא is a condition on the first line, not a separate case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two lists in the ברייתא are not two separate cases. The second list tells us when the first list works. Read this way, the ברייתא says exactly what שמואל says.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches (this is how to read it)
When are these words said? (in which case does this apply)

phrases.english: This is what the ברייתא is teaching:
When is this said?
When he says: "that which I eat of yours," "that which I taste of yours"

steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereads the ברייתא so that its second part limits the first.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to give two separate cases that each work alone.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first phrases work only together with the eating phrases, which fits שמואל.

steps.title: Another ברייתא lists the phrases in the reverse order
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא lists the eating phrases first and 'I am avowed from you' last. The second list cannot explain the first, so 'I am avowed from you' seems to work alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: But another ברייתא teaches it the opposite way: 'That which I eat of yours,' 'that which I taste of yours': forbidden. 'I am avowed from you,' 'I am separated from you,' 'I am distanced from you': he is forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 11 with a ברייתא that lists the phrases in the opposite order.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this ברייתא, 'I am avowed from you' comes after the eating phrases. So it cannot be read as the explanation from step 11. It looks like a separate case that works by itself, which goes against שמואל again.

keyTerms.meaning: But it was taught in a ברייתא
The opposite, the reverse order
I am avowed (another way to say מודר אני)

phrases.english: But it was taught in a ברייתא the opposite way:
"that which I eat of yours"
"that which I taste of yours": forbidden
"I am avowed from you" and "I am separated from you"
"I am distanced from you": he is forbidden!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 11, and so attacks שמואל again.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading from step 11 and שמואל's rule.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Here the 'I am avowed' list comes last and has its own 'forbidden'. A list that comes after cannot be explained by the list before it, so it seems to work alone.

steps.title: Changing the ברייתא's wording: 'and he already said I am avowed'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the wording of the second ברייתא to 'and he already said: I am avowed'. This shows that the two kinds of phrases work together, which fits שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Teach the ברייתא this way: 'and he had already said: I am avowed.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by changing the wording of the ברייתא so it agrees with שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the new wording, the ברייתא is not giving 'I am avowed from you' as a separate case. The eating phrase forbids him because he had already said 'I am avowed'. So it is the combination of both phrases that creates the נדר, just as שמואל taught.

keyTerms.meaning: Teach it this way (read the ברייתא with this wording)
And he had already said

steps.confusionAlert: This answer does not explain the ברייתא differently. It actually changes the ברייתא's words.

phrases.english: Teach it this way:
"and he had already said: I am avowed"
phrases.notes: In other words, the eating words work because he had already said 'I am avowed.' The two phrases go together.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Changes the wording of the ברייתא (תני הכי).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The reversed ברייתא seemed to make 'I am avowed from you' work by itself.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about someone who had already said 'I am avowed', so both phrases are present, which fits שמואל.

steps.title: The fix makes the second ברייתא repeat the first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the changed wording from Step 13. That reading makes the second ברייתא say the same thing as the first, and it does not explain why 'forbidden' is said twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, this is the same as the first ברייתא! And also, why does it need to say 'forbidden' and then 'forbidden' again?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks its own answer from Step 13. It gives two problems with the new wording of the second ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First problem: if both lists must be said together, the second ברייתא teaches nothing new beyond the first ברייתא. Second problem: the ברייתא says 'he is forbidden' after each list. That repetition shows these are two separate cases that each work alone, which goes against the old reading of שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if we accept what you just said)
This is the same as the first one (no new teaching)
And furthermore (a second problem)
Why does it need to teach this?

steps.confusionAlert: This קשיא is not against the ברייתא. It is against the גמרא's own answer in Step 13, and in the end against the way we first understood שמואל.

phrases.english: If so, this is the same as the first one!
phrases.notes: 'The first one' is the first ברייתא from Steps 10 and 11, which we already read as saying the phrases work together.

phrases.english: And furthermore:
Why does it need to teach 'forbidden' and then 'forbidden' again?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the changed wording of the second ברייתא proposed in Step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in Step 13, and with it the first reading of שמואל (that 'מודר אני ממך' only works together with the eating phrase).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The changed wording turns the second ברייתא into a repeat of the first, and it ignores the double 'forbidden,' which shows two independent cases.

steps.title: שמואל's words reread: only the one who vows is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a new reading of שמואל. Saying 'that which I eat of yours' explains why only the person vowing is forbidden while his friend stays permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, שמואל said this: the reason he is forbidden and his friend is permitted is that he said 'that which I eat of yours' or 'that which I taste of yours.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops its earlier reading of שמואל and explains what שמואל really meant. His words were about who is forbidden, not about whether the vow takes effect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier reading said 'מודר אני ממך' does nothing unless the eating phrase is added. That reading could not survive the ברייתות. In the new reading, the eating phrase points the vow at himself ('I eat'). So only he is forbidden from his friend's food, and the friend may still benefit from him.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (dropping the earlier idea for a new one)
The reason
Forbidden
His friend is permitted

steps.whatToRemember: In the end, שמואל is not saying the vow phrases fail on their own. He is explaining that 'that which I eat of yours' makes the vow one-sided: the speaker is forbidden, and his friend stays permitted.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think שמואל changed his mind. The גמרא is saying we misunderstood him before. 'אלא אמר שמואל' means 'rather, this is what שמואל actually said.'
steps.whyThisMatters: It changes the question of the whole discussion. It is no longer about whether the vow works at all. It is about who the vow forbids, the speaker or both people.

phrases.english: Rather, שמואל said:
The reason is that he said
'that which I eat of yours,' 'that which I taste of yours,'
that is why he is forbidden and his friend is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem from Step 14 by changing the reading of שמואל rather than the wording of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the אמורא's statement (changing what שמואל meant)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל meant that 'מודר אני ממך' and similar phrases do not take effect unless the eating or tasting phrase is added.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל meant that the eating or tasting phrase is why only the speaker is forbidden and his friend remains permitted. Now there is no conflict with the ברייתות that let each phrase work alone.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When someone says 'that which I eat of yours' or 'that which I taste of yours,' he is forbidden and his friend is permitted.
